attribution: Agence Rol (photographic agency), via Bibliothèque nationale de France / Gallica
depicts: Black-and-white press portrait of Amadeo Peter Giannini, founder of the Bank of Italy and later chairman of Bank of America. Head-and-shoulders, three-quarter view, chin slightly raised, looking off past the camera. He wears a wide-brimmed light-grey fedora, a dark pinstripe suit with wide lapels, a stiff white detachable collar, a striped shirt and a heavily textured knitted tie. Plain pale background.
details: The face is heavy and jowly with a thick dark moustache, deep creases at the eyes and greying hair showing at the temples under the hat brim. A small round lapel pin or badge sits on the right lapel. There is a visible collar stud below the throat. The lower left corner carries emulsion damage from the original glass plate — a pale diagonal smear across the shoulder — and small white speckles are scattered over the jacket.
visible_text: None in the cropped frame.
notes: This is the standard press portrait of A. P. Giannini and the only widely circulated photograph of him in the free-licence pool. Giannini is the man Strauss and the District appealed to in 1932; Bank of America bought the first $6 million of bonds. Two other scans of the same sitting exist on Commons (uncropped Gallica plate, and a Pacific & Atlantic print) — this is the cleanest crop.

attribution: Stefan Norblin
depicts: Oil painting portrait of A. P. Giannini as an older man, head and shoulders, turned three-quarters to the viewer. Warm brown palette throughout — a brown suit against a mottled dark-olive and umber ground, with a white shirt collar and a deep red tie the only strong accent.
details: The face is lit strongly from the upper left, leaving the right side of the head in shadow; the modelling is loose and painterly. He is white-haired and clean-shaven except for a short white moustache, with heavy pouches under the eyes and a set, unsmiling mouth — a considerably older and grimmer man than in the 1927 press photograph. The artist's cursive signature is in the lower left corner. Painted after Giannini's death in 1949, so a posthumous commemorative portrait.
visible_text: Artist's signature, lower left (Norblin).
notes: A painted rather than photographic Giannini — useful if the narration wants a more formal, monumental register than the press photo allows.

attribution: BrokenSphere
depicts: Close-up of a dark bronze National Historic Landmark plaque set into a pale granite wall at 552 Montgomery Street, San Francisco. The plaque fills nearly the whole frame and is divided into three panels by raised horizontal bars.
details: The bronze is heavily patinated to a flat charcoal with the raised lettering polished lighter. The granite surround is speckled grey-white and visibly weathered along the joint above the plaque. The photo is slightly soft — a handheld shot, but every line of text is legible.
visible_text: BANK OF ITALY / (LATER BANK OF AMERICA) / HEADQUARTERS FROM 1908 TO 1921 / FROM HERE A.P. GIANNINI LAUNCHED / THE BRANCH SYSTEM THAT TRANSFORMED / THE NATURE OF BANKING IN CALIFORNIA — NATIONAL HISTORIC LANDMARK — THIS SITE IS OF NATIONAL SIGNIFICANCE IN COMMEMORATING THE HISTORY OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA / 1982 / NATIONAL PARK SERVICE / UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR
notes: Explicitly spells out the Bank of Italy → Bank of America lineage and names Giannini. A cheap way to establish who the bank was without narration having to do it.

attribution: Bureau of Engraving and Printing
depicts: The face of a United States $5 National Currency note issued by the Bank of Italy National Trust and Savings Association, San Francisco. Engraved oval portrait of Benjamin Harrison at left, ornate blue Treasury seal at right, blue serial numbers and charter number over black engraving on cream paper.
details: Wide margins of empty cream paper above and below the printed area; a soft vertical crease runs down the centre-left. The charter number 13044 is overprinted large in blue on both sides of the bank name. Two hand-signed autographs appear at the bottom — the cashier's and, at right, 'James A. Bacigalupi, President'. The paper is lightly foxed at the edges but the note is clean and uncirculated-looking.
visible_text: NATIONAL CURRENCY / SECURED BY UNITED STATES BONDS DEPOSITED WITH THE TREASURER OF THE United States of America / SERIES OF 1902 / 263775 / 13044 / BANK OF ITALY / NATIONAL TRUST AND SAVINGS ASSOCIATION / WILL PAY TO THE BEARER ON DEMAND / FIVE DOLLARS / San Francisco CALIFORNIA February 26, 1927 / CASHIER / James A. Bacigalupi, PRESIDENT
notes: Literal money issued by Giannini's bank, dated three and a half years before the bond vote. Note the phrase 'SECURED BY UNITED STATES BONDS' — a bonus if the narration is on the subject of what a bond actually is. Very wide aspect (2.3:1), so it will letterbox or need a full-bleed crop.

attribution: G. A. Bronstrup
depicts: Pen-and-ink newspaper caricature of William Woods, General Manager of the Bank of Italy, San Francisco. A large drawn head dominates the centre; below it Woods sits at a desk signing a paper, with vignettes arranged around him — an inset panel of a golfer mid-swing at upper left, a carload of people motoring over a hill at upper right, a bank interior with a teller window at left, a pile of bulging money sacks and a stack of documents at lower right, and a small caricatured figure with a cane at lower left.
details: The desk front is lettered 'GENERAL MANAGER — BANK OF ITALY — SAN FRANCISCO'. The paper he is signing is labelled DRAFT. The money bags are marked with dollar signs and the stack beside them is labelled SECURITIES. The little figure at lower left speaks in a balloon. Signed 'Bronstrup' at lower right. Crisp black line on white — a clean, high-contrast image that will hold up at any size.
visible_text: GOLF? YEP! · ALSO AUTOING · YOU STRIKE THE KEY-NOTE OF HIS SUCCESS WHEN YOU SAY 'EFFICIENCY' · GENERAL MANAGER BANK OF ITALY SAN FRANCISCO · DRAFT · SECURITIES · Bronstrup · WILLIAM WOODS / General Manager Bank of Italy
notes: 1918 San Francisco newspaper art. Not Giannini himself, but a period visual vocabulary for the Bank of Italy — desk, drafts, money sacks, securities — that a narration about banking and bond-buying can lean on.

attribution: Publichall
depicts: Modern colour photograph of a surviving Bank of Italy branch building on a street corner in Roseville, California. A single-storey ochre-yellow classical bank block with a red tile hipped roof, tall dark plate-glass windows between pilasters, and carved white cornice panels. Crape myrtle in hot pink flower at the left edge, orange daylilies in planters along the base, empty pale concrete plaza in the foreground.
details: Two small ornamental brackets shaped like pennants are mounted on the corner pilaster. A small bronze plaque is fixed to the pier left of the entrance. Black bollards and a yellow tactile pavement strip in front mark this as a present-day pedestrian street. Two figures in light shirts stand under the trees at the far left. Hard midday sun, deep blue cloudless sky.
visible_text: Small bronze plaque beside the door (text not legible at this resolution).
notes: One of the branch-system buildings Giannini's plaque credits him with — a physical trace of the branch banking that made Bank of America big enough to buy the bonds. Contemporary photograph, so it reads as 'this still stands', not as period footage.

attribution: Franco Folini
depicts: A very wide panorama of a five-panel glass mosaic mural flanking the entrance of a Bank of America building in San Mateo, California. The panels are dense, jewel-coloured abstract-figurative compositions built from small tesserae — farm workers, a horse-drawn wagon, orchards, fishing boats, a dam, a bridge tower, cathedrals and world landmarks, and at the far right a tree and figures at a savings counter. A glass door with the street number 300 is set in the centre panel; two black planters of red and white cyclamen sit at the base.
details: The leftmost panel shows an orange-and-red fire above a horse-drawn wagon — the 1906 earthquake and fire, from which Giannini famously carried the bank's cash out of the ruins. Lettering is worked into the mosaic itself: 'A.P. GIANNINI 1870–1949' and 'THE LITTLE FELLOW'S BANK' on the left panel, a dedication line above the door, 'GIANNINI FOUNDATION OF AGRICULTURAL ECONOMICS' and 'SCHOOL SAVINGS' on the right. A tall white suspension-bridge tower against blue tesserae appears in the centre-right of the middle panel. Two ceiling lights flare into the lens.
visible_text: A.P. GIANNINI 1870-1949 · THE LITTLE FELLOW'S BANK · HIS ACHIEVEMENTS WERE THE RESULT OF HIS UNDERSTANDING OF THE NEEDS OF HIS FELLOW MAN · GIANNINI FOUNDATION OF AGRICULTURAL ECONOMICS · SCHOOL SAVINGS · 300
notes: A 1963 corporate memorial to Giannini. Extreme 2.9:1 panorama — will not fill a 16:9 frame; best used as a slow horizontal pan or cropped to a single panel. The phrase 'The Little Fellow's Bank' is exactly the self-image Bank of America wanted, and is worth quoting against the fact that homeowners had pledged their properties.

attribution: Harris & Ewing, photographer
depicts: Four men in dark business suits lean over a polished wooden desk, all looking down at a single typed document spread open in front of them. All four are smiling. A fifth figure stands half out of frame at the right. Behind them a frosted window and a hung dark curtain; the room is plain and official.
details: A leather-bound folder and a small bundle of papers held together with a metal clip sit on the desk at left. Every man has both hands flat on the desk or on the document. The desk top is dark and glossy enough to mirror the papers. The photograph is a Harris & Ewing press negative — sharp, evenly lit by flash, with the plate edge visible as a black border on all four sides. The occasion was counsel for Transamerica — Giannini's holding company — filing court action to restrict a Securities and Exchange Commission inquiry.
visible_text: None in frame; the caption is archival, not burned in.
notes: The one usable 'lawyers and a document' image tied directly to Giannini's financial empire. Dated 1939, so after the bridge was open, but generic enough to stand for the boardroom-and-litigation register this theme otherwise has almost nothing for. Use with care if the narration implies it is the 1930s bridge litigation — it is not.

attribution: R. Edgren, San Francisco Examiner
depicts: A newspaper pen-and-ink political cartoon. A long-haired, bearded man in a frock coat stands in profile with one foot planted firmly on a hairy, shaggy face lying on the ground, grinding it underfoot. To the right, a small hairy creature labelled 'S.P.' is sprawled on its back with its legs in the air, apparently kicked away.
details: The figure is Congressman James G. Maguire, an anti-Southern Pacific politician; the letters S.P. are drawn large on the flank of the flung creature. The head under his boot has staring eyes and a bristling moustache. The linework is loose and scratchy, printed on visibly coarse newsprint with the halftone screen and paper fibres showing. A second cartoon panel is cropped off at the top right, its lettering only partly readable.
visible_text: Signed 'R. Edgren '98' lower left. Caption below: 'MR. MAGUIRE'S STAND ON THE RAILROAD QUESTION.' On the creature at right: 'S.P.' Partial cropped text upper right: 'AL... NO... EV...'
notes: Twenty-five years before the Bridge District, but this is the only period cartoon in the free pool that visualises Southern Pacific as a thing to be stamped on — the standard California image of SP as the octopus/political bully that the bridge fight inherited. Tall portrait (1:1.6), so it will need cropping or a vertical pan.

attribution: Wikimedia user Liesel
depicts: A modern schematic route map of the Southern Pacific railroad system across the western United States. Green lines trace the SP network over a pale yellow land mass with red state boundaries and a solid blue ocean; major cities are marked with small squares and named in black.
details: The network fans from San Francisco and Oakland on the left edge — labelled and shown as the hub — north to Portland via the Siskiyou and Shasta routes, east over the 'Overland Route' through Ogden to a purple Union Pacific connection, and south through Los Angeles and El Paso along the 'Sunset Route' to New Orleans, with the SSW (Cotton Belt) branches through Texas and Missouri. Mexico is labelled 'MEXIKO' (German-language original).
notes: Not a period artefact — a modern reference diagram. Its use here is scale: it shows how much railroad the company that sued the bridge district owned, and that San Francisco Bay was its western terminus, which is why the ferry franchise mattered so much to it.
visible_text: Route names and city names throughout: Overland Route, Sunset Route, Union Pacific, SSW, SPCSL, San Francisco, Oakland, Sacramento, Portland, Ogden, Los Angeles, El Paso, Houston, New Orleans, MEXIKO.

attribution: Southern Pacific Railroad
depicts: Both sides of a small printed card — a Southern Pacific pocket ferry timetable — photographed side by side on a plain ground. Each side is dense black type on ageing buff card, ruled into boxed tables of departure times.
details: Left card: two tables, 'SAN FRANCISCO–SAUSALITO, Effective April 1, 1938' with boats every 20–30 minutes from 5:00 AM to the last boat at 10:30 PM, a 22-minute crossing, and fares of 15c one way / 25c round trip; below it 'SAN FRANCISCO–OAKLAND PIER', 18-minute crossing, boats every 15 minutes. Right card: the Ferry Building terminal schedule via Northwestern Pacific passenger boats, 35-minute crossing, with footnote symbols for Saturdays, Sundays and holidays, and an advertisement line for onboard facilities. The card corners are rounded and slightly furred; a crease crosses the top of the left card.
visible_text: SAN FRANCISCO–SAUSALITO / Effective April 1, 1938 / Crossing Time 22 Minutes / Foot Passengers One Way 15c Round Trip 25c / Extra Service When Traffic Demands / TRUCKS: Highway Load Limits Carried / SAN FRANCISCO–OAKLAND PIER / Crossing Time 18 Minutes / (FERRY BLDG. TERMINAL) Via N. W. P. Passenger Boats (Auto Carrying Capacity Limited.) / Crossing Time 35 Minutes—Foot passengers carried / HOLIDAY SERVICE IN THIS TIME TABLE will be operated on: New Year's, Washington's Birthday, Decoration Day, July 4th, Labor Day, Thanksgiving and Christmas / SAVE TIME :: EAT ON THE BOAT / RESTAURANT : WASHROOMS : NEWS STAND / SMOKING ROOMS ON ALL BOATS / SOUTHERN PACIFIC GOLDEN GATE FERRIES, LTD. / C. F. Fennema, General Manager / G. E. Collins, Traffic Agent / General Offices 65 Market Street, San Francisco, Calif.
notes: The single best artefact in this pool for the ferry monopoly: the company's own name — SOUTHERN PACIFIC GOLDEN GATE FERRIES, LTD. — printed at the bottom, with the exact San Francisco–Sausalito crossing the bridge was about to kill. Dated April 1938, ten months after the bridge opened, which makes it a document of a business already losing.

attribution: Unknown publisher (period postcard)
depicts: A hand-tinted picture postcard of the Southern Pacific ferry boat OAKLAND under way on San Francisco Bay. The white double-ended ferry runs broadside across the frame, low grey-green water below, a soft blue and cream sky with painted clouds above. A pier and buildings are just visible at the far left edge; a smaller vessel with masts lies beyond the ferry's stern at right.
details: The ship's name OAKLAND is painted large on the white hull side, with 'SOUTHERN PACIFIC' lettered smaller on the deckhouse above it. Two ranks of windows run the full length of the superstructure. A single tall black funnel with a whistle pipe rises amidships, and a walking-beam engine housing is visible behind it. The tinting is characteristically flat — the sky and water are washed colour over a black-and-white photographic base.
visible_text: Printed in red script at upper left: 'Southern Pacific Ferry Boat "Oakland." San Francisco, Cal.' On the hull: OAKLAND · SOUTHERN PACIFIC
notes: The ferry monopoly as it advertised itself: a big, comfortable, company-branded boat. Earlier than the bridge fight (1900s–1910s) but the boats and the business model were the same ones fighting the bridge twenty years later.

attribution: Unknown publisher (period postcard)
depicts: Colour postcard: the Southern Pacific ferry SACRAMENTO steaming from right to left across San Francisco Bay in the foreground, with the completed San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge stretching across the whole background. Pale turquoise sky, deep blue water, white wake curling off the stern.
details: The ferry's white hull is lettered 'SOUTHERN PACIFIC' with 'SACRAMENTO' beneath it. Heavy black smoke pours from the single funnel and drifts back across the bridge deck behind. The bridge's west suspension spans, the central anchorage pier and the cantilever section are all visible, with hills and a distant shoreline beyond. A lifeboat is slung on the ferry's upper deck; a figure stands at the rail near the bow. The card has a white border and a small crease at the upper right corner.
visible_text: On the hull: SOUTHERN PACIFIC / SACRAMENTO
notes: The composition does the argument for you — a Southern Pacific ferry dwarfed by, and running under, a bridge. Postwar, so it is a Bay Bridge rather than a Golden Gate image; check that the narration does not need it to be the Golden Gate.

attribution: Scanned from C. J. Allen, 'The Steel Highway' (1928)
depicts: Black-and-white halftone photograph of a Southern Pacific passenger train being loaded onto a train ferry at Port Costa. A steam locomotive with tender stands at left on multiple parallel tracks laid across a heavy timber apron; behind it a string of passenger cars runs back into the ferry slip, and the ferry's tall wheelhouse rises above the train at right.
details: 'SOUTHERN PACIFIC LINES' is lettered on the tender flank. The ferry's pilot house carries the vessel's name in large letters (partly obscured — reads as OLAND / SOLANO). Four or five railwaymen in light shirtsleeves and caps stand between the tracks watching the loading. Tall smokestacks and framed gantries clutter the middle distance. The whole plate is a coarse book halftone — the screen dots are visible and the tonal range is short.
visible_text: On the tender: SOUTHERN PACIFIC LINES. On the ferry wheelhouse: partial vessel name, '...OLAND' / SOLANO.
notes: Southern Pacific moving entire trains by boat because there was no bridge — the concrete form of the interest a bridge threatened. Small (856px long edge) and coarse-screened; fine at moderate size, will not stand a big crop. Wide 1.9:1.

attribution: Sanborn Map Company, via Library of Congress (sanborn00813 002-12)
depicts: Detail of an 1887 Sanborn fire insurance map showing the San Francisco ferry house and its slips. Seven long U-shaped ferry slips project up into the pale blue water of the bay across the top of the sheet; below them the ferry house building is drawn in yellow wash and subdivided into labelled rooms. The sheet is photographed slightly askew against a black ground, so the map is tilted a few degrees.
details: Each slip is individually named across the drawing: 'N. PACIFIC COAST R.R. FERRY SLIP', 'SAN RAFAEL & TIBURON FERRY SLIP', two 'OAKLAND FERRY SLIP', 'OAKLAND FERRY SLIP (Sacramento)', 'OAKLAND FERRY SLIP (Creek Route)' and 'ALAMEDA FERRY SLIP (S. Pacific Coast R.R.)'. The building band is lettered 'SOUTHERN PACIFIC R.R. CO'S OAKLAND FERRY' straight across it, with individual rooms marked WAITING ROOM, TICKET OFFICES, BAGGAGE RM., POST OFF., FRUIT STAND, NEWS STAND, STEAMER STORE, PRIVY, CLOCK TOWER. The block number 1517½ is printed large in the middle. Colour is limited to yellow (frame construction), pale blue (water) and grey line work.
visible_text: BAY OF SAN FRANCISCO · N. PACIFIC COAST R.R. FERRY SLIP · SAN RAFAEL & TIBURON FERRY SLIP · OAKLAND FERRY SLIP · OAKLAND FERRY SLIP (Sacramento) · OAKLAND FERRY SLIP (Creek Route) · ALAMEDA FERRY SLIP (S. Pacific Coast R.R.) · SOUTHERN PACIFIC R.R. CO'S OAKLAND FERRY · FERRY HOUSE · TICKET OFFICES · WAITING ROOM · 1517½
notes: A cadastral drawing of the monopoly: seven slips at the foot of Market Street, most of them Southern Pacific's, each one a toll gate on the way into San Francisco. Dated 1887 — establishes how long the arrangement had been in place before the bridge.

license: Flickr: No known copyright restrictions (San Francisco Public Library). Commercial use requires permission from the San Francisco History Center.
attribution: San Francisco History Center, San Francisco Public Library
depicts: Black-and-white photograph taken low from the water: the Southern Pacific Golden Gate ferry LAKE TAHOE steams left to right in the right foreground while, behind and to the left, the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge stands half-built — one completed white lattice tower at right with cables strung over its saddle, and at the far left a bare concrete pier still under construction with cranes and a derrick on top.
details: The ferry's hull is lettered in full: 'SOUTHERN PACIFIC GOLDEN GATE FERRIES LTD' along the deck edge and 'LAKE TAHOE' below it. Two large air horns and a single funnel trailing dark smoke sit on the upper deck; one small figure is visible on the bridge wing. The main cables sag between the finished tower and the unfinished pier with a slack pilot rope hanging free. Barges and a tug lie alongside the unfinished pier. The sky is a flat grey wash and the print has a soft chemical stain in the upper centre; the photograph is a period contact print with a visible paper edge.
visible_text: On the ferry hull: SOUTHERN PACIFIC GOLDEN GATE FERRIES LTD · LAKE TAHOE
notes: The most on-the-nose image in the pool: the named ferry company sailing under the bridge that will replace it, still under construction. Dated 29 November 1935, i.e. exactly the period between the bond sale and the openings. Note the rights line — SFPL asks for a credit and restricts commercial reuse.

attribution: Roger Sturtevant, Historic American Buildings Survey
depicts: Fort Point, the brick Civil War fort at the San Francisco shore of the Golden Gate, seen from the south-west with the unfinished south tower of the Golden Gate Bridge rising directly behind it. The tower is two bare concrete legs joined by a steel strut, topped with rebar cages, formwork and a tall lattice creeper crane. A row of Depression-era cars is parked along the fort's flank; raw excavated earth, rubble and a concrete-lined pit fill the foreground.
details: The fort's dark brick walls are trimmed with pale granite quoins at every corner; three tiers of narrow casemate embrasures run the length of the south wall. Guy wires from the tower crane run down past the fort in several directions. To the far left, across the water, the Marin shore and the north tower's steel falsework are visible. A steel service trestle runs off to the right behind the fort. Small temporary sheds and a construction shack stand between the parked cars and the wall. About a dozen 1930s automobiles are lined up nose-in.
visible_text: Burned into the negative: '38-P193-1' at lower right; 'CAL., 38-SANFRA, 4-1' at lower left; 'HABS' bottom centre.
notes: Fort Point is the War Department land — the Department that held Fort Point and Lime Point, feared a collapsed bridge would bottle up the harbour, held the 1924 hearings, and transferred the land. This is the clearest image of that ground with the bridge going up over it. Near-duplicate 'Fort Point 1934.jpg' also exists on Commons; this HABS version was kept for the caption text and resolution.

attribution: Published portrait, California State Library collection
depicts: Formal studio portrait, printed in warm sepia, of James Rolph Jr. — Mayor of San Francisco 1912–1931 and Governor of California 1931–1934. Head and shoulders, three-quarter turn, looking slightly off camera. Dark suit, high white wing collar, patterned dark tie with a stickpin, and a white carnation in the lapel.
details: He is bald across the crown with hair swept back at the sides, and wears a full dark moustache. The lighting is soft studio lighting with a vignetted dark background falling away behind the right shoulder. The whole image carries a fine diagonal halftone screen from the printed original, most obvious across the flat background. The white carnation — Rolph's trademark — is the brightest thing in the frame.
visible_text: None.
notes: Rolph was mayor when the Bridging-the-Golden-Gate Association was formed and when the District Act passed, and Governor of California through the 1930–33 bond crisis. This is the standard formal portrait of him.

attribution: Los Angeles Times photographic archive
depicts: Black-and-white press photograph of James Rolph Jr. in 1928, head and shoulders, standing in a doorway and smiling slightly at the camera. He wears a pale cream three-piece suit with a dark tie and a large white rose in the buttonhole; behind him is a dark panelled door and moulded frame.
details: Bright outdoor daylight from the left blows out the white shirt collar and the flower. His face is fleshy and cheerful, hair thinning and white at the sides, eyebrows dark. The pale suit against the near-black doorway makes an unusually strong figure/ground separation — good for cut-outs. Slight print grain and a few dust specks.
visible_text: None.
notes: Rolph in 1928 — the year the District was finally incorporated after five years of litigation. A warmer, more approachable image of the same man than the formal 1915 portrait; useful if the narration wants the boosterish politician rather than the office-holder.

attribution: California State Library
depicts: Governor James Rolph Jr. seated at a cluttered desk, pen in hand, signing a document, while thirteen or fourteen people — mostly men in suits, two women at the left — crowd behind and around him watching. An office interior with a framed painting and a doorway visible behind the group.
details: Rolph wears a light tweed suit with a white flower in the buttonhole and round spectacles. The desk is covered in papers, an open ledger, a desk lamp with a tilted green shade, a small vase of flowers, an inkstand and a shallow bowl. Two of the standing men lean forward with hands on the desk edge; one at the right holds a hat and a satchel; another points. Nobody looks at the camera except one man at the far right. A hand-inked negative number is scratched into the lower right corner of the plate.
visible_text: Hand-scratched plate number at lower right, partly legible.
notes: The generic bill-signing tableau — legislation, witnesses, a crowd around a desk — for the legislative side of this theme (the Bridge and Highway District Act, the 1925 and 1931 amendments). It is NOT documented as a bridge-related signing, so do not caption it as one. 800px on the long edge, the smallest keeper in the pool.

attribution: Bain News Service
depicts: Glass-plate press photograph of a woman in a large feathered hat and a light tailored jacket dropping a folded ballot into a ballot box. A man's hand and sleeve reach in from the left, holding a second ballot; another pair of hands steadies the box at the right. The box itself — a big cylindrical galvanised drum lying on its side, with a slot along the top and a number stencilled on the end — takes up the lower half of the frame.
details: The sitter is Mrs James Rolph Jr. She wears a high lace jabot at the throat and a white glove on the hand at the slot, and is smiling with her eyes down at the box. Behind her hangs a striped curtain — the polling place is improvised in a domestic or storefront room. Below and in front of the ballot drum are several kerosene lamps with glass chimneys and, nearest the camera, three men's dark felt hats resting brim-up on a table. The plate is captioned in white hand-lettering on the top edge and again along the bottom.
visible_text: Hand-lettered along the top of the negative: 'MRS. JAS. RALPH JR. VOTING'. Partly legible repeat along the bottom edge. Stencilled numerals on the ballot drum end: '...515'.
notes: The only 'a citizen actually voting' image found for this theme. It is San Francisco 1911, not the November 1930 bond election, and it is a suffrage-era publicity photo of the mayor's wife — so it can stand for the act of voting but should not be captioned as the bond vote. Tall portrait 1:1.4.

license: Public domain (marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT by the Internet Archive)
attribution: Official Souvenir Program, Golden Gate Bridge Fiesta, 1937
depicts: A single printed page from the 1937 Fiesta programme: a large oval halftone portrait of Angelo J. Rossi, Mayor of San Francisco, centred on a cream page inside a decorative scalloped border. Head and shoulders, dark suit, patterned tie, white shirt.
details: Rossi is bald on top with white hair at the sides and a clipped white moustache, faintly smiling. The oval vignette fades to black at its edge. A small engraver's union stamp reading 'I.P.E.U. 38' is printed inside the picture area at the right. Two lines of caption sit beneath the oval. The scalloped 'rope' border runs the full perimeter of the page.
visible_text: HON. ANGELO J. ROSSI / Mayor of San Francisco / Honorary Chairman, Golden Gate Bridge Fiesta. Engraver's mark: I.P.E.U. 38.
notes: Rossi succeeded Rolph as mayor in January 1931 and held the office through the whole financing crisis — the Depression, the failure to sell the bonds, and the 1932 appeal to Giannini. Sourced from the opening-celebration programme, so the page framing is celebratory rather than political.

attribution: Sydney W. Taylor, Jr., Consulting Engineer — 'The Golden Gate Bridge at San Francisco: Report of the Traffic Engineer', September 1935
depicts: The scanned opening spread of a 1935 engineering report. The left half of the spread is a blank cream page; the right half carries a simple double-ruled rectangular box near the top containing four lines of sans-serif type, the whole rest of the page empty.
details: The scan shows the physical object rather than a clean facsimile: the gutter runs as a dark vertical band down the centre, the bottom edge of the right-hand page is a black scanning shadow, and a faint library 'DOCUMENTS' stamp is just visible in the top right corner. The type is a light 1930s geometric sans — the same modernist lettering used on the bridge's own signage.
visible_text: The Golden Gate Bridge at San Francisco / REPORT OF THE TRAFFIC ENGINEER / SYDNEY W. TAYLOR, JR. / SEPTEMBER, 1935. Faint library stamp: DOCUMENTS.
notes: A title page — quiet, textual, and exactly the kind of paper that decided this project. Pairs directly with opposition-money-24, which is the one plate inside it.

attribution: Sydney W. Taylor, Jr., Consulting Engineer — Golden Gate Bridge Traffic Study, 1935, Plate 6
depicts: A large folded engineering plate: a street map of San Francisco with the primary and secondary approach routes to the Golden Gate Bridge overprinted in heavy red lines. The base map is a fine grey-black street grid on aged yellowed paper; the Presidio and Golden Gate Park are drawn as open areas at left; the bridge and toll plaza are drawn in grey at the top left, the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge in grey at the right.
details: Percentages of annual vehicular traffic are printed at points along the routes — 100.00% at the bridge itself, 80.13% and 65.01% along the northern approaches, 34.72%, 30.29%, 19.87%, 15.12% at other counting points, and '1.13% Interchange Between Bridges'. A legend box at left lists five traffic origin–destination centres and distinguishes primary from secondary approach routes. A 'STREET GRADES' key at right bands the streets by gradient (0–5%, 5.1–10%, 10.1–18%, over 18%). The paper is browned along the fold lines and the plate is photographed still bound in, with the book's board visible at the left edge.
visible_text: Header: 'Golden Gate Bridge Traffic Study—1935' · 'Plate 6'. Title block: 'PRIMARY AND SECONDARY APPROACH ROUTES IN SAN FRANCISCO — Showing per cent of Annual Vehicular Traffic apportioned to each and centers of traffic'. TAYLOR JR. CONSULTING ENGINEER.
notes: Note the label near the top right: 'S.P.–GOLDEN GATE AUTO FERRIES' — the bridge's own traffic engineer mapping the competitor's terminal. The plate is also a clean visual of where the traffic was expected to come from, i.e. the revenue that would service the bonds.

attribution: Cover illustration by Chesley Bonestell; E. Cromwell Mensch, 'The Golden Gate Bridge: A Technical Description in Ordinary Language', San Francisco, 1935
depicts: The printed front cover of a 1935 public pamphlet, in two colours only: black ink on bright orange stock. A dramatic low-angle pen illustration of the completed Golden Gate Bridge fills the upper three-quarters — looking north under the deck from the San Francisco side, the near tower rising at centre, the far tower small in the distance, the main cable sweeping down and away, and the massive dark mass of the south anchorage and Fort Point block at lower left. Two tiny figures stand on the shore at lower right for scale.
details: The drawing is dense cross-hatching and stipple; the orange shows through as the sky, the water and the roadway surface. A steel trestle and derrick are drawn at the bottom left. The illustrator's signature 'Chesley Bonestell' is at the lower left of the picture area. A black caption panel across the foot carries the title in heavy condensed white capitals with the subtitle beneath in orange. A ruled black key-line frames the whole cover, with an orange margin outside it. The paper is bright and the ink solid — this is a well-preserved copy.
visible_text: THE GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE / A TECHNICAL DESCRIPTION IN ORDINARY LANGUAGE. Signed: Chesley Bonestell.
notes: The bridge sold to the public — a cheap orange pamphlet in ordinary language, illustrated by Bonestell (later famous for space art), issued while the bridge was still being built and the bonds still had to be paid. Tall portrait, 1:1.56.

attribution: E. Cromwell Mensch, 'The Golden Gate Bridge: A Technical Description in Ordinary Language', 1935, p. 64
depicts: A single letterpress page of body text headed 'ORGANIZATION AND FINANCING', four paragraphs of dark serif type in a wide single column on cream paper, page number 64 at the foot. No illustration.
details: The type is well-inked and sharp; the right-hand edge of the sheet and the next leaf are visible at the far right of the scan. This is the page that spells out the whole financial mechanism in plain language: the enabling act, the six counties, the $35,000,000 ceiling, the two-thirds majority, the 15%-of-assessed-valuation limit, the 40-year maximum bond life and the 5% interest cap — and, in the last paragraph, the fact that the ferry lines would not be discontinued and that the toll schedule was pitched below the ferries' 99.3c average.
visible_text: ORGANIZATION AND FINANCING … 'known as the "Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District", and includes all of the City and County of San Francisco, the Counties of Marin, Sonoma, and Del Norte, and some 98% of Napa and 32% of Mendocino Counties.' … 'This estimate, not to exceed $35,000,000, together with the plan of the project, was submitted to the voters of the District. Under the requirements of the law for a two-thirds majority of all the voters, the bond issue was carried, authorizing the District to issue bonds up to the $35,000,000 limit.' … 'not to exceed 15% of the assessed valuation of the district … the maximum life of the bonds is to be 40 years … a rate not to exceed 5% per annum.' … 'the estimated construction cost was placed at $26,715,000 in the latter part of 1935.' … 'the average toll per vehicle in effect at that time on the San Francisco-Marin ferry lines was 99.3c. These ferry lines will not be discontinued upon completion of the bridge, and, anticipating competition, one of the schedules prepared was somewhat lower than this. The bridge is scheduled to be thrown open for traffic in the early part of 1937.' Page number 64.
notes: The strongest single document for this theme. It names all six member counties with the exact fractions of Napa and Mendocino, states the $35M figure, and — in its own words — frames the toll as a competitive weapon against the ferries. Text-heavy portrait page: it will need to be shown as a zoom onto a paragraph rather than a full page at 16:9.

attribution: E. Cromwell Mensch, 'The Golden Gate Bridge: A Technical Description in Ordinary Language', 1935, inside back cover
depicts: The pamphlet's back-cover 'VICINITY MAP', printed in black line on a stippled pink-buff ground inside a black keyline, with the bright orange cover stock showing as a broad border. The map covers the Golden Gate: San Francisco's street grid at the bottom, the Presidio and Golden Gate Park at lower left, the strait across the middle, and Sausalito and the Marin hills at the top. A single heavy black line runs the length of the map as the bridge and its approach highway.
details: Arrows label the key points: FORT PT. and TOLL PLAZA on the San Francisco side, LIME PT. on the Marin side, the TUNNEL and MARIN CO. HIGHWAY LEADING TO WALDO POINT to the north, ROAD TO SAUSALITO branching east, and APPROACH TO SOUTH THROUGH PRESIDIO and APPROACH TO MARINA on the city side. A compass rose and a scale bar marked to one mile sit at the centre right. Note that the map's title block, scale and several labels are set rotated 90° (reading bottom-to-top) against a page whose geography is otherwise north-up, so the sheet reads as a landscape map printed on a portrait page.
visible_text: VICINITY MAP · SCALE 0 – ¼ – ½ – ¾ – 1 MILE · SAUSALITO · MARIN CO. HIGHWAY LEADING TO WALDO POINT · TUNNEL · ROAD TO SAUSALITO · GOLDEN GATE · LIME PT. · GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE · TOLL PLAZA · FORT PT. · APPROACH TO SOUTH THROUGH PRESIDIO · APPROACH TO MARINA · SAN FRANCISCO
notes: This map labels both Fort Point and Lime Point — the two federal military reservations the War Department controlled and had to transfer before anything could be built. If the narration needs to show where that land was, this is the image. Portrait 1:1.55 with a strong orange field; text runs partly sideways, so plan the framing.

attribution: E. Cromwell Mensch, 'The Golden Gate Bridge: A Technical Description in Ordinary Language', 1935
depicts: A pen-and-ink bird's-eye panorama of the San Francisco Bay region drawn as if seen from high above the Pacific looking east, printed inside a plain ruled box on cream book paper. The Pacific Ocean and a rising sun occupy the top of the frame; the hills and city grids are rendered entirely in fine parallel hatching and cross-hatching, with the water left as blank paper.
details: Labels are lettered by hand into the drawing: PACIFIC OCEAN across the top, SAN FRANCISCO on the peninsula, MARIN COUNTY across the strait, SAN FRANCISCO BAY filling the left middle, and small leader-line captions for GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE (with an arrow at the strait), SAN FRANCISCO–OAKLAND BAY BRIDGE and EXPOSITION SITE — the last marking the future Treasure Island. A north arrow points to the right edge. Both bridges are drawn in as fine lines, the towers as small uprights. The book's gutter and the edge of the facing page are visible along the bottom of the scan.
visible_text: PACIFIC OCEAN · SAN FRANCISCO · MARIN COUNTY · SAN FRANCISCO BAY · GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE · SAN FRANCISCO-OAKLAND BAY BRIDGE · EXPOSITION SITE · N
notes: This plate was printed sideways on a portrait page; it has been rotated 90° clockwise here so it reads correctly, giving a true landscape image (1.55:1). A wide regional establishing shot in period line-art — useful for placing the six-county district geographically, though it does not draw county boundaries.

attribution: Supreme Court of the United States, October Term 1941, No. 1235; John L. McNab, counsel for petitioner
depicts: The scanned cover sheet of a United States Supreme Court filing, photographed from microfilm — dense black type on a mottled grey ground, with the dark edge of the page and a black surround visible around it. A blackletter heading 'In the Supreme Court' sits at the top; below it the term, the docket number, a ruled brace enclosing the case caption, then the document title and counsel's name.
details: At the top right a rubber-stamped box reads 'Office - Supreme Court, U.S. / FILED / MAY 14 1942 / CHARLES ELMORE CROPLEY / CLERK', with a handwritten check mark struck through the word FILED. A large handwritten '19' is looped in ink at the top centre. The case name is set in small capitals inside a hand-ruled bracket. The microfilm reproduction is low-contrast and slightly blurred at the edges but every line is readable.
visible_text: In the Supreme Court OF THE United States / OCTOBER TERM, 1941 / No. 1235 / GOLDEN GATE BRIDGE AND HIGHWAY DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA (a public corporation of the State of California), Petitioner and Appellant Below, vs. UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, Respondent and Appellee Below. / PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI to the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and BRIEF IN SUPPORT THEREOF. / JOHN L. McNAB, 300 Montgomery Street, San Francisco, Counsel for Petitioner. / Stamp: Office - Supreme Court, U.S. FILED MAY 14 1942 CHARLES ELMORE CROPLEY CLERK
notes: Litigation as a physical object: the District against the United States, all the way to the Supreme Court. This particular suit is 1942 (after the bridge opened, over federal land) rather than the 1920s Southern Pacific suits, so it is not the case named in the research — use it as the visual register of 'the project spent its life in court', or caption it precisely. Counsel's address, 300 Montgomery Street, is a block from the old Bank of Italy headquarters at 552 Montgomery.

license: Public domain (marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT by the Internet Archive)
attribution: Official Souvenir Program, Golden Gate Bridge Fiesta, San Francisco, May 27 – June 2, 1937, p. 25-A
depicts: A two-column page of printed text from the 1937 Fiesta programme, headed in a large script 'Bridging the Golden Gate' with the sub-head 'THE STORY BEHIND THE CONSTRUCTION OF THE SPAN', enclosed in the programme's scalloped rope border. Clean sans-serif body type on cream stock, page number 25-A at the foot. No illustration.
details: This is the project's own chronology, printed for the opening. It runs from Emperor Norton's 1869 proclamation through O'Shaughnessy inviting Strauss in 1917, Welch's 1919 resolution, Strauss's 1921 sketch, the Santa Rosa mass meeting of 13 January 1923 and the Bridging-the-Golden-Gate Association, the 1921 Coombs bill, the 1924 Army Engineers hearing and War Department approval, the litigation that delayed incorporation until December 1928, Strauss's appointment as chief engineer in 1929, the taxes levied on district taxpayers, the shipping interests' special hearing on clearances, the November 1930 bond vote, the taxpayers' suit and its 1932 resolution, and the start of construction on 5 January 1933.
visible_text: Key sentences: 'The Army Engineers held a hearing in San Francisco May 16, 1924.' · 'On December 20, 1924, Secretary of War John W. Weeks notified the committee of the War Department's approval of the project. Actual incorporation of the Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District was delayed by litigation instigated by opposing interests until December 1928.' · 'Subsequently, in accordance with provisions of the bridge act, a three cent tax was levied on taxpayers and later a two cent tax.' · 'Shipping interests asked a special hearing on the clearances, which was held by the Army Engineers June 30, 1930. On August 11 the same year the War Department issued the final permit fixing the clearances.' · 'In November 1930, the proposal for a $35,000,000 bond issue was submitted to the voters of the counties comprising the district, and the issue carried overwhelmingly. Bidding plans were prepared, and first bids received in July 1931. A taxpayers suit followed before the work was awarded, and a final court decision favoring the district was given in July 1932.' · 'On January 5, 1933, actual construction of the Bridge was begun.' Page number 25-A.
notes: The official narrative of the opposition, printed by the winners in 1937 — note the careful passive phrasing 'litigation instigated by opposing interests', which never names Southern Pacific. Every date the research excerpt needs is on this one page, so it can be quoted on screen as well as illustrated. Text-dense portrait page: zoom on a paragraph rather than showing it whole.
